paras: The lynching of John Gilbert was the hanging of a Black man by neighbors of a wounded white planter near Pinckney Landing, Arkansas, about thirty miles south of Memphis, in July 1903. Gilbert, charged with being implicated in the shooting of the planter H. J. Hubert, had been bound over by a magistrate when a mob took him from the officers and hanged him to a tree. The story ran as a wire item in more than two dozen white papers, while a second Black man, Jim Hawke, was named as the actual shooter and became the subject of a governor's reward.

According to a Memphis dispatch of July 22, H. J. Hubert, described as 'a prominent white planter,' was shot near Pinckney Landing. Gilbert, 'a negro,' was charged with being implicated in the shooting together with another Black man, Jim Hawkes, whom the same dispatch called 'the real author of the tragedy.'

A posse captured Gilbert and brought him before a magistrate, who bound him over to the criminal court. Neighbors of Hubert then took him from the officers and hanged him to the limb of a tree close to the scene of the shooting. The Memphis wire placed the lynching on Monday afternoon, July 20, and said Hubert died the afternoon after it.

A separate dispatch from Marion, Arkansas, dated July 23, gave a different sequence. In that version Hubert had died the day before, the magistrate had committed Gilbert to jail at Marion, and the officers taking him there were 'overpowered' and Gilbert 'strung to a limb' at Catfish Point at daybreak. The Marion report also said Jim Hawkins, 'who did the shooting,' had not been captured.

No arrest of anyone in the mob, inquest or prosecution appears in the coverage. On August 7 the Newark Journal reported that the governor had offered $100 for the arrest and conviction of Jim Hawke, 'colored,' wanted in Crittenden county for the murder of Hubert, whose initials it gave as 'W. H.' The notice described Gilbert only as 'Hawke's accomplice,' who 'was captured and lynched a few days after the crime was committed.'

Only white papers carried the story, and most printed the Memphis wire with little change. Southern dailies headlined it 'Negro Is Lynched in Arkansas Town' in Birmingham, 'Lynched for Murder' in Montgomery and 'John Gilbert Lynched' in Atlanta. The Birmingham Age-Herald's subhead said Gilbert 'shot and killed' Hubert, although the dispatch beneath it said only that he was 'implicated' and pointed to Hawkes as the real shooter.

Papers elsewhere framed the item as part of a series: the Worcester Spy headed it 'Another Negro Is Lynched in the South,' the Waterbury Evening Democrat 'Same Old Story,' and the Wheeling Register misplaced it as 'Negro Lynched in Tennessee.' The Barre Daily Times in Vermont, after quoting a South Carolina paper's sneer about another lynching, noted that the Arkansas victim was only 'alleged' to be 'implicated' and wrote, 'Still the devilish work goes on.'

By the last week of July the story had passed into syndicated weekly news digests from Wisconsin and Minnesota to Pennsylvania, Maryland, Missouri, Mississippi and Texas. In these digests the charge hardened into fact: one version said Gilbert 'killed a white planter,' another that he was lynched 'for murdering a white planter.' No report in the Black press was found.

The accounts disagree on when and where the lynching took place: the Memphis wire said Monday afternoon near Pinckney Landing, before Hubert died, while the Marion dispatch said daybreak at Catfish Point, after his death. They also disagree on Gilbert's part in the shooting, which the wire called being 'implicated,' the Marion dispatch and the reward notice attributed to Hawkins or Hawke, and later digests stated as Gilbert's own killing of the planter.

reader.title: Lynching of John Gilbert
bases: Gilbert, held by officers after a magistrate bound him over, was taken from them by Hubert's neighbors and hanged to a tree (A1, A3, A5).

Gilbert was hanged after being taken from officers who held him under a magistrate's commitment (A1, A3); the killers are called 'neighbors of Hubert' and an 'Arkansas Mob' who 'overpowered' the officers, with no number given (A1, A3, A5), and they acted on the charge that he was implicated in shooting Hubert (A1, A2).

A Memphis wire (A1, A2, A4) and a separate Marion, Ark., dispatch (A3) agree that Gilbert was taken from officers and hanged, and an Arkansas reward notice two weeks later refers to his capture and lynching (A28); they differ on the date, the place name and who did the shooting.

accounts.label: Memphis wire
accounts.gist: News reached Memphis July 22 that Gilbert, charged with being implicated in Hubert's shooting, was taken from officers by Hubert's neighbors Monday afternoon and hanged near the scene; Hubert died the next afternoon; Jim Hawkes was thought the 'real author'.

accounts.label: Marion dispatch
accounts.gist: Dated July 23 at Marion: Gilbert was lynched at Catfish Point at daybreak after officers taking him to jail were overpowered; Hubert had died the day before; Jim Hawkins 'did the shooting'.

accounts.label: Reward notice
accounts.gist: The governor's $100 reward named Jim Hawke as wanted for Hubert's murder and described Gilbert as Hawke's accomplice, captured and lynched a few days after the crime.

framing.detail: Southern papers ran the Memphis wire under headlines such as 'Negro Is Lynched in Arkansas Town' and 'Lynched for Murder', the Birmingham headline stating Gilbert 'shot and killed' Hubert while the text said only he was 'implicated'.
Northern dailies headlined it 'Another Negro Is Lynched in the South' and 'Same Old Story'; the Wheeling Register placed it 'in Tennessee'.
The Barre Daily Times stressed that the man was only 'alleged' to be 'implicated' and wrote 'Still the devilish work goes on'.
Boilerplate weekly digests turned the charge into fact: 'who killed a white planter' and 'for murdering a white planter'.

conflicts.note: The Memphis wire is the most widely carried; the Marion dispatch is datelined at the county seat to which Gilbert was being taken, so neither is clearly better evidence.
